strengths: The proposed method, CLEAR, introduces a simple yet elegant two-parameter calibration scheme to dynamically balance and scale epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty estimates in a data-driven manner.

The paper provides an extensive empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets and diverse variants, demonstrating a significant reduction in prediction interval width (NCIW) and quantile loss compared to individually calibrated baselines, while strictly maintaining the nominal coverage.
The proposed 'ALEATORIC-R' baseline, which fits quantile regression on residuals of the median predictor, is a valuable and stable contribution to the estimation of aleatoric uncertainty.

The combination of the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework for epistemic uncertainty with Conformalized Quantile Regression (CQR) for aleatoric uncertainty is well-motivated and thoroughly executed.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with highly detailed appendices containing comprehensive results, theoretical discussions (including finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees for a split-sample variant), and a practical case study.
weaknesses: The computational complexity of the framework is quite high, as it requires training ensembles for the PCS epistemic uncertainty estimator and multiple bootstrap models for the aleatoric part. This may limit scalability to very large datasets or complex deep learning models.

The theoretical novelty is somewhat incremental. The core combination is a linear additive combination of the two uncertainty types, and the asymptotic validity proof heavily relies on standard consistency assumptions of the base estimators.

To maintain strict, finite-sample distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees, the data must be split into train, validation, and calibration sets. Reusing the validation set for calibration works well empirically but technically forfeits the exact finite-sample guarantee (though the authors show in Appendix G how to recover it with an additional split).
The presentation of the different variants (a, b, c) in Section 3.3 is slightly dense and could be simplified to improve readability for general readers.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and important problem: how to properly balance and scale epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty components when constructing prediction intervals.

The proposed CLEAR framework is highly flexible, allowing any epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty estimators to be plugged in. The integration with the PCS (Predictability-Computability-Stability) framework and CQR on residuals is well-designed.

Extensive empirical evaluation is conducted across 17 diverse real-world datasets, demonstrating consistent improvements in both interval width and quantile loss while maintaining the desired coverage.

The paper provides both synthetic simulations showing improved conditional coverage in extrapolation regions, as well as a practical case study (Ames Housing) illustrating how the learned trade-off parameter $\lambda$ adapts to feature availability.

The manuscript is well-written, thoroughly documented, and contains comprehensive theoretical discussions (including asymptotic conditional coverage and finite-sample marginal coverage for a split-validation variant) in the appendix.
weaknesses: In the default implementation of CLEAR (Algorithm 1), the validation set $D_{\text{val}}$ is reused as the calibration set $D_{\text{cal}}$. Although the authors show this doesn't hurt empirical coverage, it technically violates the exact finite-sample distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees of standard conformal prediction. While the 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant in Appendix G.1 resolves this, this distinction should be made more prominent in the main text.

The computational cost is relatively high, as estimating the epistemic uncertainty via PCS requires training bootstrap ensembles ($b=100$), followed by fitting quantile regression models on the residuals. This could limit scalability to massive datasets or very large neural network models.

The main empirical comparisons (e.g., Figure 3) omit UACQR (Rossellini et al., 2024), which is acknowledged as the conceptually closest baseline. Although UACQR results are present in the appendix tables, bringing a direct comparison into the main text would have strengthened the presentation of CLEAR's advantages.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated objective of combining both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty sources to improve the conditional coverage of prediction intervals.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets and synthetic simulations with 10 random seeds, demonstrating favorable results on interval width and quantile loss compared to several baselines.
Thorough appendix containing detailed explanations, multiple variants of the base models (variants a, b, and c), and a detailed case study on the Ames Housing dataset.
The proposed residual-based aleatoric estimator (ALEATORIC-R) shows solid empirical benefits over direct quantile regression on the targets.
weaknesses: Limited Technical Novelty: The methodology is conceptually straightforward. It essentially applies standard split conformal prediction using a locally adaptive scaling function defined as a linear combination of aleatoric and epistemic estimators: \(\sigma_\lambda(x) = \hat{q}^{ale}(x) + \lambda \hat{q}^{epi}(x)\). Tuning the mixing parameter \(\lambda\) on a validation set using pinball loss is an incremental extension of existing conformal UQ literature (such as UACQR).

Invalidation of Conformal Guarantees in Default Setting: In the recommended default setting, the authors reuse the validation set for conformal calibration (\(D_{val} = D_{cal}\)). While this improves data efficiency, optimizing \(\lambda\) and calibrating \(\gamma_1\) on the same dataset violates the exchangeability of conformity scores. Consequently, the default method lacks the rigorous finite-sample distribution-free coverage guarantees that make conformal prediction appealing.

High Computational Overhead: To estimate the epistemic uncertainty via the PCS framework, the user must train a large ensemble of models (e.g., 100 bootstrap models) across multiple data perturbations. Additionally, the method requires running a grid search over 4,000 points of \(\lambda\). This significant computational cost makes the framework difficult to scale to massive datasets or deep learning architectures.

Overstated Contribution on Residual Fitting: Contribution 2 claims that fitting quantiles on residuals is a novel contribution of this work. However, fitting auxiliary models (or quantile regressors) on residuals to capture heteroskedasticity is a long-standing and widely used technique in locally adaptive conformal prediction.

Strong Theoretical Assumptions: The asymptotic conditional validity in Lemma 2.1 relies heavily on the consistency of both the base models and the quantile regression estimators, which is rarely achievable in practice on finite, high-dimensional, or noisy real-world datasets.

strengths: Addresses a key open challenge in uncertainty quantification (UQ) by providing a unified, data-driven approach to scale and balance both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties.

The proposed method, CLEAR, is highly modular and flexible. It can be wrapped around any arbitrary pair of epistemic (e.g., PCS ensembles, Deep Ensembles) and aleatoric (e.g., CQR, SQR) uncertainty estimators.

Optimizing both the scale parameter (\(\gamma_1\)) and the trade-off parameter (\(\lambda\)) via pinball/quantile loss on a validation set is well-justified, leveraging the property that the true conditional quantiles minimize the expected quantile loss.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 17 diverse real-world regression datasets shows consistent, substantial improvements in interval width (NCIW) and quantile loss over strong baselines, while rigorously maintaining nominal coverage.

The Ames Housing case study beautifully illustrates the interpretability of the learned parameter \(\lambda\), demonstrating how CLEAR adaptively shifts weight toward aleatoric uncertainty when predictive features are removed, and toward epistemic uncertainty when using all features.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with a highly detailed appendix containing extensive reviews of related work, intuitive theoretical motivations, and complete experimental tables.
weaknesses: The asymptotic conditional validity guarantee (Lemma 2.1) relies on strong consistency assumptions for both the PCS base estimators and the quantile regression models, which are generally difficult to guarantee or verify in finite-sample, high-dimensional settings.

Applying the fully conformalized version of CLEAR (as detailed in Appendix B.1 and G) requires dividing the validation data into separate validation and calibration splits, which can lead to a data-efficiency trade-off and potential parameter overfitting on smaller datasets.

The linear/additive combination of the two uncertainty estimators is a specific structural choice. While intuitive and effective, the paper does not extensively explore or discuss alternative formulation shapes (e.g., quadratic combination, which is common in physics/error propagation, or non-linear scaling).

strengths: Highly practical and well-motivated framework (CLEAR) that successfully integrates and balances aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for regression tasks.

The two-parameter calibration formulation (γ1 for coverage scale and λ for the trade-off ratio) is elegant: by computing γ1 via conformal calibration for each candidate λ, the method guarantees valid marginal coverage while enabling the optimization of the interval's shape using a proper scoring rule (quantile loss) on validation data.

Extremely thorough empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets with multiple base models (PCS with QRF, QXGB, Expectile GAM) and modern deep learning models (Deep Ensembles + SQR), demonstrating consistent improvements in interval width (NCIW) and quantile loss.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with a very detailed appendix (67 pages) containing extensive theoretical justifications, thorough ablation studies, and runtime analyses.
Clear demonstration of conditional coverage improvements in out-of-distribution and extrapolation regions through synthetic simulations.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: combining epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties via scaling parameters has been explored in prior work (such as Rossellini et al., 2024, which fixes γ1 = 1). Nonetheless, the joint data-driven optimization of both parameters while maintaining coverage is a highly practical contribution.

The claim that fitting quantiles on the residuals provides much more sensible estimators of aleatoric uncertainty than fitting directly on the targets is presented as a major novel insight, but fitting noise or quantile estimators on residuals is already a well-established practice in heteroskedastic regression and conformal prediction.

The default implementation of CLEAR reuses the validation set for both calibration and parameter selection (D_cal = D_val), which technically breaks the finite-sample distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees of conformal prediction. Although the authors present 'Conformalized CLEAR' (using a separate split) in Appendix B.1, this distinction and its theoretical implications should be discussed more prominently in the main text.

The computational cost of the PCS ensemble (requiring fitting 100 bootstraps across multiple base models) is relatively high compared to standard CQR. While the modularity of CLEAR allows for cheaper estimators, the computational overhead of the primary implementation should be explicitly acknowledged in the main text.

strengths: Strong Empirical Performance: The proposed CLEAR method is extensively evaluated across 17 real-world regression datasets, consistently outperforming standard conformal baselines (like CQR) and epistemic-only baselines (like PCS) in terms of normalized calibrated interval width (NCIW) and pinball loss, while maintaining the correct marginal coverage.

Simple, Post-hoc, and Modular Design: CLEAR is highly modular and can be wrapped around any existing epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty estimators (as demonstrated with PCS + CQR, and Deep Ensembles + SQR). The two-parameter calibration optimization via a fast 2D grid search is computationally efficient and very practical.

Thorough and Extensive Appendix: The authors provide a very comprehensive supplementary material including detailed descriptions of related work, theoretical justifications of the pinball loss properties, extensive tabular results across all configurations, and detailed runtime analyses.

Intuitively Appealing Trade-off: The case study on the Ames Housing dataset nicely demonstrates how the method adapts to different information regimes, prioritizing aleatoric uncertainty when fewer features are available and epistemic uncertainty when more features (and thus complex model structures) are used.
weaknesses: Incremental Methodological Novelty: The core proposal is to scale and sum two existing uncertainty estimates. This is conceptually very close to UACQR (Rossellini et al., 2024), which corresponds to fixing the first scaling parameter to 1 and tuning only the relative ratio. Allowing both parameters to be free is a relatively straightforward extension, even if the paper shows it provides a practical boost in robustness.

Theoretical Limitations of the Asymptotic Validity: Lemma 2.1 proves asymptotic conditional validity under the assumption that the epistemic uncertainty converges to 0 point-wise as the training set grows. However, if the epistemic term vanishes asymptotically, the asymptotic conditional validity is achieved solely because the aleatoric estimator is consistent. Thus, the lemma does not theoretically justify the benefit of combining both uncertainties over simply using a consistent aleatoric estimator.

Overstated Novelty on Residual-Based Quantile Regression: The authors list as their second contribution the demonstration that fitting quantiles on the residuals provides much more sensible estimators of aleatoric uncertainty than fitting the quantiles directly on the targets. While this is indeed a useful design choice, estimating quantiles of residuals is a well-established technique in the heteroskedastic regression, regression diagnostics, and conformal prediction literature.

Computational Complexity of PCS: The primary framework used for epistemic estimation, PCS, relies on bootstrapping and multiple pre-processing pipelines, which can be computationally prohibitive for very large datasets or deep learning architectures.
